ab-wheel-rollout.name: Ab Wheel Rollout
ab-wheel-rollout.execution: Kneel on a pad, grip the ab wheel handles with arms straight below your shoulders. Brace your core HARD — imagine someone is about to kick you in the stomach. Roll the wheel forward slowly, keeping the lower back FLAT (no arch). Extend as far as you can while maintaining that flat-back position — maybe 12 inches, maybe full extension. Pull back using your lats and abs together — don't just snap the hips. Return to start. Reset the brace before the next rep.
ab-wheel-rollout.why: The ab wheel rollout trains anti-extension — the core's ability to resist the lower back arching under load. In hockey, this is the mechanism that lets you generate a powerful slap shot or body check without your spine collapsing. Anti-extension core strength, not crunches, is the key to a resilient hockey spine.
ab-wheel-rollout.transfer: Advanced anti-extension — builds elite core stiffness. Ab wheel exposes core weakness instantly. The truth is unforgiving. Embrace the data.
ab-wheel-rollout.cues: "Start kneeling" · "Roll out slow" · "Hips stay level" · "Pull back with lats and core"
ab-wheel-rollout.mistakes: Arching the lower back at extension — kills the benefit and compresses lumbar discs. Using hips to snap back — the pull should come from the abs and lats. Going to full extension before you have the strength — earn it over weeks. Holding your breath — brace and breathe (short exhale on the way out, inhale on return).
ab-wheel-rollout.progression: Progress: Standing ab wheel rollout from feet (instead of knees) — elite-level anti-extension demand. | Regress: Dead bug — same anti-extension demand but from the floor with zero spinal loading.

bird-dog.name: Bird Dog
bird-dog.execution: Start on all fours — hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Spine neutral. Brace the abs slightly — don't suck in, BRACE outward. Simultaneously extend the RIGHT arm forward and LEFT leg back. Both limbs reach parallel to the floor. Hold 3-5 seconds. Return to start WITHOUT letting the spine rotate or dip. Switch sides. Alternate for 8-10 reps per side.
bird-dog.why: The bird dog is the #1 movement control drill for building lumbar spine stability — essential for hockey players with lower-back issues. By extending the opposite arm and leg simultaneously, you train the deep core stabilizers (multifidus, QL) to hold the spine neutral under load. Every hockey player should do this daily; back injuries are the #1 cause of missed games in the NHL.
bird-dog.transfer: Trains spinal stability and balance — foundation for all dynamic movement. More spine-injury-prevention research behind this movement than almost any other. Take it seriously.
bird-dog.cues: "On all fours" · "Extend opposite arm and leg" · "Hold 2 seconds" · "Keep hips level"
bird-dog.mistakes: Rotating the hips to lift the leg higher — the spine must stay perfectly still. Rushing — hold each rep 3-5 seconds. Speed kills the benefit. Letting the lower back arch — keep it neutral; rib cage down. Only doing it when your back hurts — prevention is the point.
bird-dog.progression: Progress: Bird dog with a band on the extended arm — adds instability demand. | Regress: Dead bug — same anti-rotation demand from a supine position, easier to feel spine position.

dragon-flag.name: Dragon Flag
dragon-flag.execution: Lie on a sturdy flat bench, head at one end. Grip the edge of the bench BEHIND your head with both hands. Brace the core. Drive your feet up to the ceiling so your body is vertical — only shoulders and upper back contact the bench. Lower your ENTIRE body as one rigid line — feet, hips, and shoulders all descending together. Stop the descent 1-2 inches before your feet touch the bench. Pause. Reverse direction. The bench is your anchor only — body never relaxes against it. Shoulder blades stay planted. 3-6 strict reps per set. Quality only.
dragon-flag.why: The dragon flag is the single most demanding anti-extension movement in the strength world — popularized by Bruce Lee and used by every elite gymnast and combat athlete. Unlike a plank where you hold a static position, the dragon flag requires the entire body to move as ONE RIGID PLANK through an enormous range of motion — from vertical down to nearly horizontal — while the rectus abdominis fights gravity's attempt to break the body at the hip. For hockey, this builds full-trunk-rigidity strength at a level no other exercise reaches: the kind of bombproof core that lets a player absorb a hit while accelerating, hold the puck on the boards under contact, or fire a slap shot while being checked. The catch: it's brutally hard. Most players need 6-12 months of progressions to earn a clean rep.
dragon-flag.transfer: The single hardest anti-extension movement in strength training. Builds rectus, spinal stabilizers, AND lats in one move — full-body trunk strength under maximum lever load. Bruce Lee's signature. Earn this exercise. If you can't hold a 60-second hollow body hold, you're not ready — work that progression first.
dragon-flag.cues: "Lie on a bench" · "Grip behind your head with both hands. Lift body to vertical (shoulder blades stay planted). Lower the WHOLE body as one straight line — no breaking at the hip. Stop just before touching" · "Then raise back up."
dragon-flag.mistakes: Breaking at the hip on the way down — body must stay straight as a board; if hips drop first, regress. Touching the bench at the bottom — that's resting; stop 1-2 inches above and control the eccentric. Skipping the progressions — this exercise will break your lower back if you cheat the prerequisites. Holding the breath — exhale through the hard portion; brace doesn't mean Valsalva.
dragon-flag.progression: Progress: Straight-arm dragon flag (hands gripping a fixed point in front of you instead of behind head) — even harder lever. Or weighted dragon flag with ankle weights. | Regress: Tucked dragon flag — knees bent to chest during the descent. Earn 15+ reps before extending the legs. Prerequisite: 60-second hollow body hold.
dragon-flag.muscles: Rectus Abdominis, Spinal Erectors, Lats, Glutes, Full Trunk

l-sit-hold.name: L-Sit Hold
l-sit-hold.execution: Sit on the floor with legs straight in front of you. Hands flat on the floor by your hips, fingers pointing forward. Press hard into the floor — depress your shoulders, lock arms straight, lift your butt off the ground. Lift your legs straight off the floor until they're horizontal — body forms an L. Toes pointed, quads tight, shoulders down. Look forward, not at your feet. HOLD. Breathing stays steady — don't bear down. Lower under control. Rest. Repeat.
l-sit-hold.why: The L-sit is gymnastics' brutal isometric core builder — and it's NOT just an abs exercise. To hold the body off the floor with legs horizontal, you need simultaneous strength from the abs, hip flexors, triceps, anterior shoulders, and even the quads (locked straight). It teaches the entire anterior chain to coordinate as one rigid unit under load. For hockey, the transfer is direct: the body position of an L-sit is what a player is in when they're absorbing a check while braced in a flexed position — abs locked, hips loaded, arms supporting body weight against contact. It's also one of the few exercises that builds visible-ab strength via isometric tension alone, with zero spinal flexion involved.
l-sit-hold.transfer: Gymnastics-derived isometric — abs, hip flexors, triceps, AND shoulders all firing at once. Builds the iron core required to absorb checks while braced in a flexion-loaded position. Most can't lift the butt off the floor cleanly at first — start with tuck L-sit (knees bent) until 30s, then extend.
l-sit-hold.cues: "Sit on the floor (or parallettes for full range). Hands flat by hips" · "Fingers forward. Press hard" · "Lock arms" · "Lift entire body — legs straight out horizontal in an L. Hold. Tight quads" · "Pointed toes" · "Depressed shoulders."
l-sit-hold.mistakes: Bent knees — start with tuck L-sit if you can't keep them straight; don't pretend. Shoulders shrugged up to the ears — kills the press and the position; depress them down. Tilting backward to compensate — torso stays vertical or slightly forward. Holding the breath — long isometric needs oxygen flow; breathe steadily.
l-sit-hold.progression: Progress: L-sit on parallettes — extra height lets you go from full pike to lifted position with deeper range. Then V-sit (legs above horizontal). | Regress: Tuck L-sit — knees pulled to chest during the hold. Build up to 30s clean tucks before extending the legs.
l-sit-hold.muscles: Rectus Abdominis, Hip Flexors, Triceps, Shoulders, Quads

lateral-bear-crawl.name: Lateral Bear Crawl
lateral-bear-crawl.execution: Get on hands and toes — knees hovering 1-2 inches off the floor. To move RIGHT: step right hand AND right foot OUT to the right simultaneously. Then bring left hand and left foot in to match, returning to the start position. That's one lateral 'step.' Continue 5-8 steps right, then reverse direction. Hips stay low and LEVEL — no twisting, no piking. Slow and deliberate. Same-side hand and foot move together (this is the OPPOSITE of forward bear crawl).
lateral-bear-crawl.why: The lateral bear crawl trains the sideways contralateral pattern — exactly the neural firing sequence of crossover steps on the ice. While forward bear crawls are general athletic patterning, the lateral version is hockey-specific: it grooves the same hip-and-shoulder coordination that powers tight-turn skating, edge work, and the lateral push-off used in pivots. Lateral patterns are the most under-trained athletic skill in pre-puberty athletes — most off-ice work is sagittal-plane only.
lateral-bear-crawl.transfer: Sideways bear crawl trains the lateral coordination pattern of skating + builds anti-rotation core strength. The cross-body neural patterning is GOLD for under-13 athletes. The most-under-trained pattern in pre-puberty hockey training. Most off-ice work is sagittal-plane only. Fix that.
lateral-bear-crawl.cues: "Hands and toes down" · "Knees hovering 1 inch off the floor. Hands shoulder-width. Step right hand AND right foot out sideways together" · "Then left hand and left foot follow. Keep hips low and level."
lateral-bear-crawl.mistakes: Moving same-side hand and foot at different times — defeats the pattern. Twisting the hips toward the direction of travel — should stay perfectly square. Letting one knee touch the floor — even briefly. Hover hold is the point. Going too wide on the steps — small steps train the pattern; big steps cheat with momentum.
lateral-bear-crawl.progression: Progress: Lateral bear crawl with a band around the wrists OR ankles — adds anti-collapse load. | Regress: Lateral quadruped hold (no movement, just shift weight side-to-side in the hover position).

plank-challenge-max-hold.name: Plank Challenge — Max Hold
plank-challenge-max-hold.execution: Get into a perfect plank — forearms on the floor, elbows under shoulders, body in a straight line. Glutes squeezed, core braced as if bracing for a punch. Neutral neck — look at the floor between your hands. Start the timer. Breathe in steady patterns. Hold until form breaks: hips sag, hips pike, shoulders shift — at that moment, stop the clock. Write the time down. Beat it next time.
plank-challenge-max-hold.why: The max-hold plank is the gold-standard test of core ENDURANCE — the muscle quality that holds your skating stride together in the third period. The side plank is a top predictor of low-back resilience in athletes, and front plank endurance correlates strongly with shot velocity (hockey shooters use the core as the transfer point from legs to stick). Tracking this number monthly is one of the simplest pieces of evidence that your off-ice work is paying off.
plank-challenge-max-hold.transfer: Long hold = core endurance + grit. Beat your previous time. Hockey is a long game and a strong core is what holds your stride together in the third period. Hockey is a long game. Strong core in the first period is easy; strong core in the third is the metric.
plank-challenge-max-hold.cues: "Get into a perfect plank: straight line from heels to head" · "Elbows under shoulders" · "Glutes tight" · "Core squeezed. Hold for as long as you can with PERFECT form. The second your hips sag" · "You're done. Time it. Beat it next time."
plank-challenge-max-hold.mistakes: Letting hips sag mid-hold — every second past that point is not a real plank. Holding breath — drops blood pressure, fatigues you faster. Piking hips up to make it easier — same disqualification as sagging. Testing this when fatigued — retest only fresh, ideally first thing in a session.
plank-challenge-max-hold.progression: Progress: Weighted plank challenge — plate on the upper back, same protocol. | Regress: Knee plank challenge — same form but with knees on the floor instead of toes.

russian-twist.name: Russian Twist
russian-twist.execution: Sit on the floor, knees bent, heels on the floor or elevated for more difficulty. Lean back until the torso is at 45° — feel the core engage to hold this position. Hold a weight (plate, med ball) or clasp hands together. Rotate the torso fully to the right — weight reaches toward the floor beside the hip. Rotate left. That is one rep. Keep the lower back from rounding — stay tall through the chest.
russian-twist.why: The Russian twist trains rotational core endurance — the ability to maintain rotational power through multiple repetitions, which mirrors the repeated stick-checking, body positioning, and puck battle demands across a full game. While it shouldn't replace heavier anti-rotation work, it builds the oblique endurance that keeps your core rotating powerfully in overtime when everyone else has faded.
russian-twist.transfer: Rotational strength and endurance — replicates rapid direction changes. Med ball or plate at chest height. The load adds stimulus, the rotation IS the exercise.
russian-twist.cues: "Lean back slightly" · "Feet off floor (harder)" · "Rotate side to side with control"
russian-twist.mistakes: Rotating only the arms — the torso must rotate, not just the hands. No weight — bodyweight is too easy for most. Use a plate or med ball. Rushing — controlled rotation with full range beats fast, sloppy movement. Lower back rounding — if it rounds, reduce the lean angle.
russian-twist.progression: Progress: Cable Russian twist standing — adds resistance and requires more bracing. | Regress: Seated rotation without lean-back — upright position reduces core demand.

stir-the-pot-swiss-ball.name: Stir the Pot (Swiss Ball)
stir-the-pot-swiss-ball.execution: Kneel in front of a stability ball. Place both forearms on the ball. Assume a plank position — hips lifted, body in a straight line. Move the forearms in small circles — clockwise and counter-clockwise. The rest of the body must stay perfectly still while the arms move. Circles should be small initially — 15-20cm diameter. 10 circles each direction per set.
stir-the-pot-swiss-ball.why: Stir the pot (forearms on a stability ball, circling the ball) is the most advanced anti-extension and anti-rotation core exercise combined. The unstable surface of the ball multiplies the core stability demand exponentially compared to a plank — small arm movements force the entire core to work continuously at high activation levels. It trains the rotational core stability needed to resist being pushed off the puck in traffic.
stir-the-pot-swiss-ball.transfer: Trains dynamic core stability under rotation — elite-level exercise. Hips don't move. Spine doesn't extend. The ball moves; you don't. That's the drill.
stir-the-pot-swiss-ball.cues: "Elbows on ball" · "Body plank" · "Move elbows in circles both directions" · "Hips still"
stir-the-pot-swiss-ball.mistakes: Hips dropping or piking — maintain the rigid plank throughout. Circles too large — bigger circles create more instability than most can control. Start small. Holding the breath — brace and breathe simultaneously. Rushing through it — slow, deliberate circles maximise core activation.
stir-the-pot-swiss-ball.progression: Progress: Larger circles or a less inflated ball — both increase instability demand. | Regress: Standard plank — master the static hold before adding the circular motion.

toes-to-bar.name: Toes-to-Bar
toes-to-bar.execution: Hang from a pull-up bar, hands shoulder-width, palms forward, dead hang. Pack the shoulders down. Brace the core. Lift straight legs slowly — through horizontal, all the way up. Pull yourself slightly back/forward to angle the body — toes connect with the bar between your hands. Lower under control over 2-3 seconds back to dead hang. 5-10 strict reps. No swinging, no kipping, no momentum.
toes-to-bar.why: Toes-to-bar is the full-range progression of the hanging leg raise — instead of stopping at horizontal, you continue lifting the legs all the way up until your toes touch the bar. That extra range adds significant lat involvement (your lats pull you slightly back to create the angle), turns it into a true full-body anti-extension drill, and crushes the rectus abdominis in a way few exercises can match. The 'advanced ab' move every elite gymnast, CrossFit athlete, and rotational-sport athlete trains. For hockey, it's the gold-standard finisher — a few sets of strict toes-to-bar train both the trunk flexion that powers shots AND the grip/lat strength needed for stick battles and puck protection.
toes-to-bar.transfer: Advanced progression of the hanging leg raise — combines full rectus chain with lat strength and grip endurance. The "advanced ab" move every elite athlete trains. Direct carryover to the trunk-flexion power needed for hard shots and fast get-ups. If you can't do strict hanging leg raises to horizontal first, sub those — toes-to-bar requires both abs AND lat strength.
toes-to-bar.cues: "Dead hang from a bar. Lift straight legs all the way UP — toes touch the bar between your hands. Lower under control. Strict reps only — no kipping" · "No swinging."
toes-to-bar.mistakes: Kipping for momentum — converts the exercise into shoulder cardio; abs do almost nothing. Bent knees — start with bent knees only if you're regressing to knee-to-bar, otherwise straight legs. Not lifting all the way to the bar — half-reps; that's just a hanging leg raise. Touch the bar or it doesn't count. Trying it before you can do strict hanging leg raises to horizontal — earn the prerequisite first.
toes-to-bar.progression: Progress: Weighted toes-to-bar — light ankle weights or dumbbell between feet. Or strict toes-to-rings for added shoulder stability demand. | Regress: Hanging leg raise to horizontal — earn 12+ strict reps before attempting toes-to-bar.
toes-to-bar.muscles: Rectus Abdominis, Hip Flexors, Lats, Grip, Shoulders

v-up.name: V-Up
v-up.execution: Lie flat on your back, arms extended overhead, legs straight together. Press your lower back into the floor — that's the start position, no arch. Simultaneously and explosively raise both your torso AND your straight legs toward each other. Reach your hands toward your toes at the top — body forms a V shape. Lower with control back to the start position. Touch the floor lightly between reps; don't relax. 10-15 reps for a working set.
v-up.why: The V-up is one of the few dynamic spinal-flexion exercises still defensible for athletes. HIGH-volume LOADED repeated flexion (i.e. weighted crunches, 50+ rep sets) is what wrecks spines, but a low-volume bodyweight V-up trains explosive trunk-flexion power — a real hockey quality. The exact muscle action of a V-up — torso and legs explosively meeting at the top — is what a player does to get up off the ice after a fall, or to sit up into a check with the trunk braced. Programmed at 10-15 reps for 3 sets, 1-2× per week, the V-up adds a useful dynamic to a spine-safe core block without the disc-load downside of high-rep crunches.
v-up.transfer: Dynamic, explosive trunk-flexion under control — the exact muscle action of getting up off the ice fast after a fall, or sitting up into a check. Low-volume, bodyweight-only keeps it spine-safe for athletes. Bent knees on the way up = cheating. If you can't keep them straight, sub a tuck-up until you can.
v-up.cues: "Lie flat on your back" · "Arms overhead" · "Legs straight. Explosively raise torso AND straight legs simultaneously to meet at the top in a V. Reach hands toward toes. Lower with control."
v-up.mistakes: Bending the knees on the way up — kills the difficulty and the stimulus; straight legs or sub tuck-ups. Letting the lower back arch as legs lower — press it into the floor through the descent. Using arm momentum to fling up — both ends move together; not arms first. Treating it as high-volume cardio — keep sets ≤15 reps and quality high. This is strength work.
v-up.progression: Progress: Weighted V-up — hold a light dumbbell or medicine ball overhead. Or candlestick V-up (legs go above vertical at top). | Regress: Tuck-up — same setup, bend knees as you rise. Build up to 15 clean tucks before progressing.

wrist-curl.name: Wrist Curl
wrist-curl.execution: Sit on a bench. Hold a dumbbell or barbell with an underhand grip (palms up). Rest the forearms on the thighs — wrists hanging over the knees. Lower the weight by extending the wrists — full stretch at the bottom. Curl the weight back up by flexing the wrists — full contraction at the top. Pause 1 second at the top. Lower slowly — 2-3 seconds. Both wrists simultaneously or alternating.
wrist-curl.why: Wrist flexion strength is the primary force producer in the wrist shot — the snap of the wrists at puck release is what separates a 75 mph shot from a 90 mph one. Wrist curls build the forearm flexors (flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris) that generate this snap. They also build the forearm mass that absorbs stick impacts during battles without injury to the tendons.
wrist-curl.transfer: Wrist flexion strength directly powers the wrist shot snap. Pair with wrist roller for full forearm coverage. Quiet day, real payoff in March.
wrist-curl.cues: "Forearms on bench" · "Wrists hanging off" · "Curl up" · "Squeeze" · "Lower slow"
wrist-curl.mistakes: Moving the forearms off the thighs — they must remain flat. Only the wrist moves. Partial range — full extension to full flexion every rep. Too heavy too soon — wrist tendons adapt more slowly than muscles. Build progressively. Neglecting the non-dominant (receiving/puck-handling) hand — both sides equally.
wrist-curl.progression: Progress: Barbell wrist curl with heavier load — progressive overload for forearm strength. | Regress: Band wrist curl — lightest load option, safe for tendon conditioning beginners.

ankle-hops.name: Ankle Hops
ankle-hops.execution: Stand with feet hip-width, arms relaxed at sides. Push off the ground using ONLY your ankles — minimal knee bend. Think pogo stick. Land on the balls of your feet and immediately bounce back up. Contact time should be minimal. Keep hips and knees relatively straight throughout. Focus on fast, light ground contact — not height. Do 10-20 consecutive hops, rest, repeat.
ankle-hops.why: Ankle hops develop the spring-like stiffness in the Achilles-ankle complex that reduces ground contact time during skating strides. Stiffer ankles mean faster energy return — like a better spring — which directly increases stride frequency and agility speed. Reactive strength index (how quickly you can absorb and return force) strongly predicts agility performance.
ankle-hops.transfer: Builds calf and ankle stiffness for faster skating push-off. Twenty contacts × three sets. Use as warm-up before bigger plyos — primes the calves and Achilles.
ankle-hops.cues: "Keep knees almost straight" · "Hop rapidly using only ankles" · "Tall posture"
ankle-hops.mistakes: Using the knees too much — this becomes squat jumps. Lock the knees and use the ankle spring. Slow ground contact — you want to 'ping' off the floor, not squat into it. Landing on the heels — kill for ankle development. Balls of feet only. Too many reps per set — quality of spring matters more than endurance.
ankle-hops.progression: Progress: Single-leg ankle hops — maximum hockey transfer for the skating push-off. | Regress: Double-leg calf raises — build the strength before the spring.

box-jump.name: Box Jump
box-jump.execution: Set the box height at a level you can land in a quarter-squat — not full squat. Stand 6-12 inches in front of the box. Feet shoulder-width. Counter-movement: arms swing back, hips dip, then EXPLODE up. Land softly on the box with both feet, in a quarter-squat. Absorb through hips. Stand fully on the box (full hip extension) — DON'T skip this. Step DOWN one foot at a time. Don't jump down — that's how Achilles tears happen.
box-jump.why: Box jumps build reactive strength — the ability to absorb force and immediately reverse direction. The TAKEOFF is what trains explosive power; the box just gives you a soft landing target. Critical for hockey because every skating stride is essentially a small unilateral box jump pattern with rapid landing absorption.
box-jump.transfer: Builds explosive vertical power — transfers to skating thrust. If you land in a deep squat, the box is too high. Athletic landing position only — slight knee bend, hips back.
box-jump.cues: "Swing arms" · "Explode up" · "Land softly with hips back" · "Step down (never jump down)"
box-jump.mistakes: Box too high — encourages hip-tucking instead of pure jump height. Pick a box where you land in QUARTER squat. Jumping DOWN at the end — load on Achilles is 8-10× bodyweight. Step down. Not standing fully upright on the box — half-reps don't count. Using box jumps as conditioning (high reps) — destroys the power adaptation.
box-jump.progression: Progress: Single-leg box jump (lateral) once bilateral version is mastered. Direct hockey crossover. | Regress: Box step-up with explosive intent on the lead leg — builds the pattern without the impact.

explosive-step-up-jump.name: Explosive Step-Up Jump
explosive-step-up-jump.execution: Stand facing a box or bench (40-60cm). Place one foot fully on the box. Drive explosively through the box foot — extend the hip, knee, and ankle. Drive the opposite knee UP as you leave the box — like a sprint drive. At the top, both feet briefly leave the box (small hop). Land back on the box foot first, absorb, and step down. Complete all reps one leg, then switch. Arms drive in opposition.
explosive-step-up-jump.why: The explosive step-up trains the single-leg concentric power pattern of the skating push-off — one leg driving the entire body upward explosively. Unlike bilateral jumps, it isolates the weaker leg's power deficit and trains the exact neuromuscular pattern of an aggressive stride. It is one of the most direct strength-to-skating transfer exercises available.
explosive-step-up-jump.transfer: Single-leg explosive power — mirrors the skating push-off. Pair with heavy split squats for a contrast complex. Heavy strength → explosive expression.
explosive-step-up-jump.cues: "Drive through one leg" · "Explode off box" · "Switch legs in air" · "Soft landing"
explosive-step-up-jump.mistakes: Pushing off the back foot on the floor — all drive must come from the box foot. Low box height — box should be at least knee height for proper loading. No arm drive — aggressive arm swing increases power output significantly. Slow, grinding reps — must be explosive. If it's slow, lower the weight.
explosive-step-up-jump.progression: Progress: Add dumbbells in each hand as bodyweight becomes easy — significant load increase. | Regress: Slow step-up — controlled ascent without the explosive hop, mastering single-leg mechanics first.

trap-bar-jump.name: Trap Bar Jump
trap-bar-jump.execution: Load the trap bar at 20-30% of your trap-bar deadlift 1RM. NOT heavier — it kills bar speed. Stand inside the bar, feet hip-width. Grip handles with arms straight. Set hips back into a 1/4 squat, chest tall, eyes forward. Drive feet through the floor explosively — bar should leave the ground 4-8 inches. Land softly with bent knees. Reset to start position before next rep. Bar speed is everything: if it feels slow, drop the load.
trap-bar-jump.why: Trap bar jump is the single most effective off-ice exercise for skating power — a staple in NHL strength programs. The trap bar's neutral grip + center-of-mass loading lets you express max velocity safely with significant load. Loaded jumps in the 20-30% 1RM range produce the highest power output across the entire force-velocity curve.
trap-bar-jump.transfer: GOLD STANDARD for skating power — loaded triple extension mimics the exact mechanics of a skating stride. The #1 hockey lift. Pair with heavy trap-bar deadlifts for a complex. Heavy strength → max-velocity expression.
trap-bar-jump.cues: "Light load (20-30% of trap bar deadlift 1RM). Quarter squat" · "Explode UP and leave the floor 4-6 inches. Land soft."
trap-bar-jump.mistakes: Going too heavy — kills the speed adaptation. If reps are slow, drop the weight. Rounding the lower back at setup — same form rules as a deadlift. Trying to land softly on toes only — distribute through the whole foot. Doing more than 5 reps per set — power decays after rep 3-5.
trap-bar-jump.progression: Progress: Cluster sets: 5 sets × 3 reps with 15s between reps — combines power output with extra volume. | Regress: Kettlebell swing first — same hip-hinge explosion pattern, lower technical demand.

vertical-jump.name: Vertical Jump
vertical-jump.execution: Stand side-on to a wall. Reach up and mark your standing reach with chalk. Swing arms back, dip into a quarter-squat — load the hips. Explode upward — drive arms, extend hips, knees, and ankles fully. At the peak, touch the wall as high as possible. Measure the difference between standing reach and jump reach. Attempt 3-5 jumps with full recovery. Record the best.
vertical-jump.why: Vertical jump height is the most widely used single measure of lower-body explosive power in hockey — used at the NHL combine as a primary athletic indicator. Every stride push-off in skating is a partial expression of vertical jump mechanics (triple extension). Research shows a 1-inch increase in vertical jump correlates with measurably faster first-step quickness and 10m sprint times on the ice.
vertical-jump.transfer: Measures and trains total lower body power output. If your vertical hasn't moved in 8 weeks, the program is wrong. Track it monthly. Honest numbers don't lie.
vertical-jump.mistakes: Too deep a squat — a quarter-squat produces more power than a full squat dip. No arm swing — the arm swing adds 2-4 inches. Always use the arms. Letting the knees cave inward at take-off — drive them outward. Not tracking progress — measure monthly. The trend matters.
vertical-jump.progression: Progress: Depth jump to max vertical — adds reactive strength demand. | Regress: Squat jump — same mechanics, no arm swing, builds the triple extension pattern.

10m-acceleration-sprint.name: 10m Acceleration Sprint
10m-acceleration-sprint.execution: Set two cones 10m apart. Start in a 3-point or 2-point athletic stance. Lean forward aggressively — your body angle should feel like you're falling. Drive the first step BACK and DOWN into the ground (not forward and up). Pump arms hard in opposition — short, powerful arm action. Stay low for the first 4-5 steps. Don't pop upright. Hit full speed as you cross the 10m cone. Time with a stopwatch or gate.
10m-acceleration-sprint.why: The 10m acceleration drill isolates the most critical skating phase — the first 3-4 strides after a standing start. This is when first-step quickness is decided. NHL analytics show that ~80% of offensive zone entries that lead to goals involve a player winning a 0-10m race. Training short accelerations specifically develops the fast-twitch motor units and ankle stiffness needed to win those battles.
10m-acceleration-sprint.transfer: Mimics the explosive 10m bursts used constantly in hockey shifts. 4-6 reps at full intent, 2-3 minutes rest. Cut the rest and you cut the adaptation.
10m-acceleration-sprint.cues: "Start in athletic stance" · "First step is long and aggressive" · "Drive arms"
10m-acceleration-sprint.mistakes: Standing upright on the first step — kills forward momentum. Stay low. Overstriding — stepping far in front of the hips brakes you. Drive DOWN, not forward. Weak arm drive — arms set the tempo for the legs. Aggressive arms = faster legs. Not recording your times — you can't improve what you don't measure.
10m-acceleration-sprint.progression: Progress: Resisted 10m with a sled or partner-held band — builds more force into the initial push. | Regress: Falling start: lean against a wall, fall forward, catch yourself with a sprint — removes the start decision and teaches aggressive forward lean.

3-point-start-sprint.name: 3-Point Start Sprint
3-point-start-sprint.execution: Place one hand on the floor in front of you. Opposite foot forward. Back leg is extended — body in a low, aggressive forward lean. Weight is distributed: ~60% front foot, 30% hand, 10% back foot. Hips are slightly above shoulder height — loaded like a compressed spring. On go: drive off the back foot AND front foot simultaneously, hand leaves the floor. Sprint hard for 15-20m. Arms pump aggressively from the very first step.
3-point-start-sprint.why: The three-point start (one hand on the floor, body in an aggressive lean) trains the most powerful acceleration starting position — used in every explosive starting situation from a whistle restart to a breakaway. The low hand position forces a forward lean angle that maximises horizontal force production in the first strides. Elite sprinters consistently produce higher acceleration from three-point versus two-point starts.
3-point-start-sprint.transfer: Trains explosive horizontal acceleration from a low position — mimics a faceoff or breakout start. Pair with falling start for full acceleration toolkit. Both teach the lean; this one adds loaded power.
3-point-start-sprint.cues: "One hand down" · "Hips up" · "Weight forward. On GO" · "Drive the first step long and aggressive. Sprint hard to the 10-15m mark — stay low for the first 5 steps. Decelerate" · "Walk back" · "Full recovery" · "Repeat. Every sprint is max intent."
3-point-start-sprint.mistakes: Hips too high — reduces the explosive drive angle. Hips at or just above shoulder height. Hand too far forward — it should be directly under or just ahead of the shoulder. Rising upright immediately — stay low for the first 4-5 strides. Weak first step — the first step must be the most explosive of the run.
3-point-start-sprint.progression: Progress: Three-point start into resisted sprint — adds sled or band for overload. | Regress: Two-point athletic stance start — master the aggressive lean before adding the hand.

40m-sprint-intervals.name: 40m Sprint Intervals
40m-sprint-intervals.execution: Mark a 40m course. Stand at the start. On your signal, sprint the full 40m at 95-100% effort. Time every rep. Target: maintain within 5% of best time across all reps. Walk or jog back to start — approximately 60-90 seconds rest. Repeat 6-10 times. Stop the session if times drop more than 10% from your best.
40m-sprint-intervals.why: 40-metre sprint intervals train the full acceleration-to-near-top-speed spectrum — the distance range of most meaningful on-ice sequences. From a defensive zone start to the opposing blue line is approximately 30-40 metres. Training this distance repeatedly develops the neuromuscular patterns, glycolytic capacity, and acceleration endurance that sustain explosive play through multiple consecutive shifts.
40m-sprint-intervals.transfer: Conditions the anaerobic system for repeated high-speed shifts. Sprint posture stays tall the whole way. The second your shoulders round forward, decelerate and walk it in.
40m-sprint-intervals.cues: "Max effort every rep" · "Full recovery between reps" · "Consistent mechanics"
40m-sprint-intervals.mistakes: Starting at 70-80% — every rep must be near-maximal. Rest too long — 60-90 second recovery is deliberately incomplete. Shorter than full recovery. Not recording times — the data tells you when to stop and how you're progressing. Running beyond 10 reps — quality degrades rapidly. Stop at 10 maximum.
40m-sprint-intervals.progression: Progress: Shorter rest (45s) once times stay consistent with 90s rest. | Regress: 20m sprint intervals — shorter distance for athletes building sprint capacity.

agility-ladder-high-knees.name: Agility Ladder — High Knees
agility-ladder-high-knees.execution: Stand at one end of the ladder, facing down its length. Drive each foot into a separate ladder box — high knee on every step. Thighs should reach parallel or above with every drive. Arms pump hard in opposition — this drives the cadence. Move forward as fast as possible while landing each foot accurately inside a box. Do not touch the ladder rungs — aim for the middle of each box.
agility-ladder-high-knees.why: Agility ladder high knees combine the hip flexor speed of high knees with the precise foot placement demand of ladder work — training both raw cadence and spatial accuracy simultaneously. This dual demand mirrors the skating situation where a player must move feet rapidly while threading through traffic. The forced accuracy at high speed builds the neuromuscular control that separates fluid skaters from choppy ones.
agility-ladder-high-knees.transfer: Improves foot speed, coordination, and neuromuscular quickness. Run the ladder fast and sloppy and you train sloppy. Slow it down, hit every box clean, repeat.
agility-ladder-high-knees.cues: "One foot per square" · "Lift knees to hip height" · "Fast arm drive" · "Stay tall"
agility-ladder-high-knees.mistakes: Low knees to go faster — height is the point. Slow down if knees drop. Looking at the feet — eyes forward once the pattern is established. Flat-footed landings — balls of feet only, every contact. Neglecting arm drive — arms set the tempo. Lazy arms equal lazy legs.
agility-ladder-high-knees.progression: Progress: Single-leg ladder high knees (hop on one foot through each box) — elite reactive demand. | Regress: Slow high knee march through the ladder — master placement before adding speed.

carioca.name: Carioca
carioca.execution: Stand sideways to the direction of travel. Going right? Left side faces forward. Step right foot to the right. Bring left foot to cross IN FRONT of right. Step right again. Bring left foot to cross BEHIND right. That's the rhythm: out, front-cross, out, back-cross — repeat. Hips rotate freely; arms swing freely; eyes look forward (not at feet). Go slowly first to nail the pattern. THEN gradually speed up.
carioca.why: Carioca trains the crossover-step pattern — the exact mechanics of hockey crossovers and tight-turn acceleration. Beyond the pattern itself, it builds hip rotation mobility under low-load conditions and develops the lateral fluidity that separates smooth skaters from choppy ones. Carioca ranks as a top general warm-up tool because it activates multiple planes of motion in a single drill: lateral, rotational, and sagittal all at once.
carioca.transfer: The crossover-step pattern — exactly how you accelerate on the ice with crossovers. Builds hip rotation, coordination, and that hockey-specific lateral fluidity. If your crossovers feel awkward on the ice, your carioca needs work. Same wiring, off-ice version.
carioca.cues: "Move sideways. Right foot crosses IN FRONT of left" · "Left steps out" · "Right crosses BEHIND" · "Left steps out. Stay low" · "Hips open and close" · "Arms swing freely. Go slow first — get the pattern" · "THEN speed up."
carioca.mistakes: Looking at the feet — destroys posture and rhythm. Eyes forward, FEEL the pattern. Locked hips — kills the rotational component. Let them swing. Same cross-direction every time (always front, never back) — defeats the alternating pattern. Going too fast before mastering the pattern — bad reps reinforce bad movement.
carioca.progression: Progress: Speed carioca — execute the same pattern at near-sprint pace. Tests true coordination. | Regress: Side-step shuffles (no crosses) — builds the lateral pattern before adding the rotational layer.

curved-sprint.name: Curved Sprint
curved-sprint.execution: Mark a circle or arc on the ground (use cones or a track curve). Radius ~5-10 metres. Sprint along the curve, leaning your whole body INTO the centre of the circle. Drive the outside foot hard laterally on every stride — push away from the centre. Inside arm pumps harder to counterbalance the lean. Maintain top speed through the entire arc — don't decelerate in the curve. Alternate direction (clockwise and counter-clockwise) equally.
curved-sprint.why: Curved sprints train the lateral force application needed for tight turns on ice — when skating a circle or arc, you must lean and push laterally, not just forward. Running curves trains the hip abductors and ankles to drive force at an angle, directly improving speed through the offensive zone circle and around-the-net plays. NHL players make curved acceleration actions 12-18 times per game.
curved-sprint.transfer: Hockey skating happens on ARCS, not straight lines. Curved sprints train inside-leg and outside-leg power asymmetry exactly like a turn on the ice. Pair with linear sprint work for full coverage. Both needed; neither sufficient alone.
curved-sprint.cues: "Set 5 cones in a 15m arc. Sprint along the curve. Inside foot pushes harder. Run BOTH directions (left and right curves)."
curved-sprint.mistakes: Running upright instead of leaning — you must lean into the curve like a speed skater. Slowing down in the curve — the curve is where speed is won or lost. Always curving the same direction — both directions equally, always. Too large a radius — tighter curves (5m) produce more lateral force and better transfer.
curved-sprint.progression: Progress: Sprint-to-cut: full speed on the curve, then plant and sprint straight — mirrors breaking out of the zone. | Regress: Jog the curve at 70% focusing on lean mechanics before adding speed.

l-drill.name: L-Drill
l-drill.execution: Set 3 cones in an L-shape: A at start, B 5 yards ahead, C 5 yards to the right of B. Sprint from A to B. Touch the base of B with your hand. Sprint back to A. Touch A. Sprint to B, then curve around B to C — run a tight figure-8 around B and C. Sprint back through B and back to A to finish. Time with a stopwatch. Elite hockey players target sub-7.0 seconds.
l-drill.why: The L-drill (3-cone drill) is one of the most widely used agility tests in North American sport — used at the NFL, NBA, and NHL combines. It tests the ability to accelerate, decelerate, and change direction around tight cones in a figure-L pattern. For hockey players it directly measures the agility required for tight-turn maneuvers, beating a defender wide, and the ability to stop and restart in confined spaces.
l-drill.transfer: Develops tight turns and directional change — crucial for dekes and edge work. Two trips both directions per session. L-drill is a TEST, not conditioning. Treat it that way.
l-drill.cues: "Attack each cone" · "Tight turns" · "Stay low" · "Drive out of each cut"
l-drill.mistakes: Wide arcs around the cones — attack each cone tightly. The difference between a good and great time is the arc. Not touching the cone base — requires a genuine hip drop, which is the athletic challenge. Standing up too soon out of each cut — stay low through the entire drill. Only timing in one direction — always run it both ways.
l-drill.progression: Progress: Reactive L-drill — coach calls direction at the start so athlete cannot pre-plan. | Regress: Walk the pattern at 50% speed, then 75%, before timing at full speed.

reactive-agility-drill.name: Reactive Agility Drill
reactive-agility-drill.execution: Set up cones in a T or Y pattern. Stand at the start. A partner or coach holds a coloured cone or ball — they will point or move to signal direction. On their signal, react and sprint to the indicated direction as fast as possible. The signal should come AFTER the athlete has started moving — forcing true reaction. Rest fully and repeat — vary signals so the pattern is never predictable. Track reaction time and direction accuracy.
reactive-agility-drill.why: Reactive agility (responding to a visual or auditory cue rather than a pre-planned movement) is fundamentally different from planned agility — it adds a cognitive component that mirrors actual game demands. Research consistently shows that reactive agility scores predict on-ice performance better than planned agility tests. Training reactive agility builds the decision-speed that allows a player to close gaps faster than the opponent can react.
reactive-agility-drill.transfer: Trains reaction time and change-of-direction speed under pressure. Pre-planned drills train footwork. Reactive drills train decisions. Hockey is a decision sport. Train the decision.
reactive-agility-drill.cues: "Stay in low athletic stance" · "React to visual cue" · "Explosive first step"
reactive-agility-drill.mistakes: Anticipating the signal — if you're always guessing right, the drill is too predictable. Slow response time — the gap between signal and first step is what's being trained. Only using visual cues — also practice auditory cues (voice commands) for game realism. Skipping rest — reactive agility is neuromuscular, not cardiovascular. Full recovery needed.
reactive-agility-drill.progression: Progress: Add a secondary task (call out a number, catch a ball) to increase cognitive load. | Regress: Planned agility drills — build the physical patterns before adding the reaction component.

resisted-sprint.name: Resisted Sprint
resisted-sprint.execution: Attach a sled (10-15% bodyweight) or band at the waist. Start in a low sprint position — forward lean, one foot forward. Drive powerfully against the resistance — lower body acceleration, hard arm drive. Stay low through the first 8-10 strides. Don't pop upright. Sprint 15-20m against resistance. Rest 2-3 minutes fully before the next rep.
resisted-sprint.why: Resisted sprinting (sled push, band, or parachute) forces the athlete to produce more horizontal force than an unloaded sprint — specifically overloading the hip extensors and ground-reaction force production that drives acceleration. Post-activation, the unresisted sprint feels lighter and faster (contrast effect). Research shows 4-6 weeks of resisted sprint training improves 10m acceleration by 3-6% — a significant edge in gaining position on the ice.
resisted-sprint.transfer: Builds explosive first-step power for breakout speed. Three steps, max effort, walk back. If your second sprint feels easier than your first, you're not pushing hard enough.
resisted-sprint.cues: "Drive knees high" · "Pump arms aggressively" · "Stay on balls of feet"
resisted-sprint.mistakes: Too much load — if you can't maintain sprint mechanics, reduce the weight. Standing upright too soon — stay low. Upright = less horizontal force. Weak arm drive — arms drive the leg tempo. Big arm action required. Short rest — this is maximal power work. Full recovery between reps.
resisted-sprint.progression: Progress: Contrast with unloaded sprint immediately after — best acceleration training combo. | Regress: Light band resistance before progressing to sled.

sled-push.name: Sled Push
sled-push.execution: Load the sled to a weight you can push for 20-30m with effort. Grip the sled handles low. Lean forward aggressively — body at 45° angle. Drive with alternating leg pushes — full extension at the hip and knee each stride. Stay low — the moment you stand up, force goes up instead of forward. Arms drive along the sled rails — keep pushing powerfully through the full distance. Walk back to start. Full 2-3 minute recovery before the next rep.
sled-push.why: The sled push is the safest and most mechanically pure acceleration exercise available — it forces a low, forward-lean drive position with maximum leg extension that directly translates to skating acceleration mechanics. Unlike sprinting, there is no eccentric landing phase, making it extremely low injury risk while allowing maximum force output. NHL strength coaches use heavy sled pushes as their primary acceleration development tool in pre-season.
sled-push.transfer: Overloads hip extension — builds the same force production as a powerful skating stride. Twenty meters out, walk back. If you finish a set fresh, you went too light. Sled push should burn the quads.
sled-push.cues: "Forward lean" · "Drive through full extension" · "Arms push sled low"
sled-push.mistakes: Standing upright — the horizontal force component is what transfers to skating. Stay low. Load too heavy — if you can't maintain drive mechanics, reduce the weight. Short steps — full hip extension on every push. No shuffling. Short rest — sled pushes are power work. Full recovery between reps.
sled-push.progression: Progress: Sprint off the sled immediately after a push — contrast effect for maximum acceleration CNS stimulus. | Regress: Empty sled or very light load — master the mechanics before adding weight.

stair-sprints.name: Stair Sprints
stair-sprints.execution: Find a staircase with 20-40 steps. Warm up at the bottom. Sprint up the stairs — drive each knee high, push off each step fully. Take one or two steps at a time — one-step drives the quad and hip; two-step drives the glute more. Arms pump hard in opposition. Walk down carefully — the eccentric descent is the injury risk, not the sprint up. Rest at the bottom 60-90 seconds before the next rep.
stair-sprints.why: Stair sprints train explosive hip flexion and triple extension simultaneously — every step requires a powerful knee drive and full push-off, exactly like an exaggerated skating stride. Stairs also force the body into a forward lean automatically, grooving the acceleration posture. They are joint-friendly due to the reduced landing impact compared to flat-ground sprinting, making them excellent in-season conditioning.
stair-sprints.transfer: High-force, low-impact conditioning — builds the power-endurance of skating. The favorite alternative to sled push when you don't have a sled. Same vertical force production demand.
stair-sprints.cues: "Drive knees" · "Pump arms" · "Sprint up" · "Walk down for recovery" · "Repeat"
stair-sprints.mistakes: Jogging instead of sprinting — every rep must be maximal effort. Running down the stairs — walk down every time. Ankle and knee risk is high going down fast. Low arm drive — aggressive arm swing adds 5-10% to stair sprint performance. Too many reps — 6-10 high-quality sprints beats 20 sloppy ones.
stair-sprints.progression: Progress: Weighted stair sprint (light vest) — adds load without changing the mechanics. | Regress: Stair step-up march — deliberate slow step-ups before adding sprint speed.

t-drill.name: T-Drill
t-drill.execution: Set 4 cones: one at start (A), one 10 yards ahead (B), one 5 yards left of B (C), one 5 yards right of B (D). Sprint from A to B. Touch the base of cone B with your right hand. Shuffle LEFT to cone C. Touch C with your left hand. Do NOT cross your feet. Shuffle RIGHT all the way to cone D (10 yards). Touch D with your right hand. Shuffle LEFT back to cone B. Touch B. Backpedal from B back to A. Stop the clock.
t-drill.why: The T-drill measures and trains the combination of acceleration, deceleration, lateral quickness, and change of direction — the exact physical demands of forechecking, gap control, and defensive zone coverage. NHL combine scouts use the T-drill as one of five primary athletic tests. Sub-4.5 second T-drill times correlate strongly with elite agility ratings from coaches.
t-drill.transfer: Classic hockey agility test — trains multi-directional change of direction. Three drills, full recovery between. T-drill is a TEST, not conditioning.
t-drill.mistakes: Crossing feet on the shuffle — illegal and slower. Stay in shuffle mechanics. Not touching the cone base — requires a full hip drop, which is the athletic challenge. Decelerating too early before the cone — attack the cone, then redirect. Running a slow, lazy warm-up version — every rep should be timed and compete against your best.
t-drill.progression: Progress: Reactive T-drill — coach points direction at cone B instead of predetermined route. | Regress: Walk through the pattern first, then 50% speed, then full speed.

agility-ladder-crossover-step.name: Agility Ladder — Crossover Step
agility-ladder-crossover-step.execution: Stand sideways to the ladder. Face one end. Lead foot steps inside the first box. Trail foot crosses OVER and lands inside the same box. Lead foot steps to the next box. Trail foot crosses over again. Move laterally down the ladder in this crossover pattern. Stay low — slight knee bend maintained throughout. Look ahead, not at the feet. Arms drive in opposition to the legs.
agility-ladder-crossover-step.why: The agility ladder crossover step trains the lateral foot speed and crossover mechanics that directly transfer to on-ice crossovers in tight turns. The crossover is the fastest turn technique in skating, and the off-ice ladder version builds the foot coordination, hip rotation, and weight transfer pattern that makes on-ice crossovers faster and more automatic.
agility-ladder-crossover-step.transfer: Trains the crossover pattern at speed — directly applies to skating crossovers. Pair with carioca for full lateral-foot-speed warm-up. Both essential, neither sufficient alone.
agility-ladder-crossover-step.cues: "Lateral movement" · "Cross lead foot over each square" · "Stay tall" · "Drive off outside foot"
agility-ladder-crossover-step.mistakes: Looking at the feet — eyes forward once the pattern is learned. Standing upright — stay in the athletic crouch throughout. Sloppy crossing — the cross-step must be deliberate and complete, not a shuffle. Only going one direction — always practice both left-lead and right-lead.
agility-ladder-crossover-step.progression: Progress: Add a lateral bound after the last ladder box — transitions from ladder to real power. | Regress: Slow walk-through of the crossover pattern — learn the foot placement before adding speed.',

agility-ladder-ickey-shuffle.name: Agility Ladder — Ickey Shuffle
agility-ladder-ickey-shuffle.execution: Stand to the side of the ladder. Begin with the near foot. Step IN with the near foot (inside the box). Step IN with the far foot (both feet inside the box). Step OUT with the near foot (outside the ladder, one box ahead). Now the far foot steps IN to the new box — cycle begins again. Build speed progressively: walk-through → jog → full speed.
agility-ladder-ickey-shuffle.why: The Ickey shuffle is a three-step lateral ladder pattern that trains the exact foot sequencing of an ice hockey crossover — in, in, out, shift, repeat. It demands simultaneous hip rotation, weight transfer, and foot speed in a lateral direction. Regular Ickey shuffle training has been shown to significantly improve lateral agility scores and correlates directly with edge-to-edge skating quickness.
agility-ladder-ickey-shuffle.transfer: Complex foot pattern that trains neuromuscular quickness and coordination. Three trips per session as warm-up. Builds the foot-speed reflex without taxing the CNS.
agility-ladder-ickey-shuffle.cues: "In" · "In" · "Out pattern — step in with lead" · "Then trail foot" · "Exit with lead" · "Keep moving"
agility-ladder-ickey-shuffle.mistakes: Skipping the walk-through phase — this pattern requires deliberate learning before speed. Arms not driving — let the arms mirror the lateral body movement. Losing the rhythm after a mistake — stop, reset, restart the pattern. Only going one direction — always practice leading with both feet.
agility-ladder-ickey-shuffle.progression: Progress: Ickey shuffle with acceleration sprint at the end of the ladder. | Regress: Lateral two-feet-in shuffle (basic lateral ladder) — simpler pattern to learn first.',

agility-ladder-lateral-in-out.name: Agility Ladder — Lateral In-Out
agility-ladder-lateral-in-out.execution: Stand sideways to the ladder. Both feet outside one end. Step both feet into the first box — in, in. Step both feet out the other side — out, out. Shuffle laterally to the next box. Repeat — in, in, out, out. Progress down the full ladder. Keep hips low throughout. Return going the opposite direction.
agility-ladder-lateral-in-out.why: The lateral in-out ladder drill trains the rapid weight transfer and hip abductor/adductor coordination that drives lateral skating acceleration. Each step in and out of the ladder forces a quick hip shift — exactly what happens during an edge change. It is one of the simplest ladder patterns but one of the most direct transfers to on-ice lateral quickness.
agility-ladder-lateral-in-out.transfer: Improves lateral foot speed and coordination for edge work. Pair with sprint work earlier in the session. Ladder primes the feet; sprints test them.
agility-ladder-lateral-in-out.cues: "Both feet in" · "Both out each square" · "Stay on balls of feet" · "Increase speed"
agility-ladder-lateral-in-out.mistakes: Standing tall — maintain athletic crouch with hips loaded. Slow, deliberate steps at full speed — build to game-speed tempo. Touching ladder rungs — aim for the centre of each box. Only training one direction — both lateral directions equally.
agility-ladder-lateral-in-out.progression: Progress: Add a resistance band at the hips for lateral resistance during the drill. | Regress: Slow controlled lateral steps through the ladder — accuracy before speed.',

backcheck-simulation-sprint.name: Backcheck Simulation Sprint
backcheck-simulation-sprint.execution: Start at one end of a 30-40m space. Simulate an offensive-zone position. On signal, sprint BACKWARDS 3-4 steps (mimic a defenseman's retreat), then pivot and sprint forward full speed. Drive arms hard, stay low through the first 5 strides. Sprint through the finish line — don't decelerate early. Walk back to start. Full recovery before next rep. Optional: add a lateral shuffle at the end to simulate getting in front of a trailer.
backcheck-simulation-sprint.why: The backcheck sprint replicates the most physically demanding defensive action in hockey — a full-speed retreat from the offensive zone. It trains both max-speed running mechanics AND the mental discipline to sprint hard when already fatigued. Analytics show teams that win the backcheck race within 3 seconds of a turnover concede 60% fewer odd-man rush goals.
backcheck-simulation-sprint.transfer: Mimics the desperate backcheck — sprint 50m at full speed from offensive zone. Defenders: this is your bread and butter. Train the recovery sprint as hard as you train the offensive sprint.
backcheck-simulation-sprint.cues: "Sprint full speed" · "Transition to backward skating simulation at midpoint" · "Sprint again"
backcheck-simulation-sprint.mistakes: Jogging instead of sprinting — this drill only works at 95-100% effort. Poor pivot mechanics — practice the turn separately until it's fluid. Stopping before the finish — commit through the line every rep. Too many reps without recovery — 6-8 quality sprints beat 15 sloppy ones.
backcheck-simulation-sprint.progression: Progress: Add a resistance band at the waist for the sprint phase — increases force production demand. | Regress: Straight 30m sprint first — nail pure sprint mechanics before adding the pivot.

backward-skater-squat.name: Backward Skater Squat
backward-skater-squat.execution: Stand on one leg. Extend the other leg slightly behind you. Hinge at the hip and bend the standing knee, lowering your body backward and down. Reach your arms forward for counterbalance as you descend. Lower until the rear knee nearly touches the floor. Drive through the heel of the standing foot to return — feel the glute fire. Complete all reps one side, then switch.
backward-skater-squat.why: The backward skater squat isolates the glutes and hamstrings in the exact hip-extension pattern of backward skating — a critical skill for defensemen and all players retreating in the defensive zone. Most players are quad-dominant; this exercise corrects that imbalance and builds the posterior chain strength that drives backward stride power.
backward-skater-squat.transfer: Mimics backward skating mechanics — essential for defensemen. Defensemen: this is your single-leg pattern. Forwards: still useful, but lower priority than Bulgarian split squat.
backward-skater-squat.cues: "Single leg" · "Lower into squat position while mimicking backward stride reach"
backward-skater-squat.mistakes: Collapsing forward at the trunk — keep a proud chest, hinge and squat simultaneously. Letting the knee cave inward — push it out over the pinky toe. Only going halfway — full range builds full-range strength. Rushing the reps — slow and controlled builds the pattern that matters.
backward-skater-squat.progression: Progress: Add a dumbbell or hold a weight plate to increase demand as bodyweight becomes easy. | Regress: Reverse lunge to a box — reduces the balance demand while building the same pattern.

faceoff-stance-explosive-start.name: Faceoff Stance Explosive Start
faceoff-stance-explosive-start.execution: Assume a faceoff stance: feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet. Hold a stick (or simulate) in the faceoff grip. Partner or coach gives a random signal (voice, clap, or ball drop). The instant you see or hear the signal, explode forward — drive off the back foot. Sprint through 5-10 metres at full speed. Reset, vary the signal timing to train reaction, not anticipation.
faceoff-stance-explosive-start.why: The faceoff is one of the most explosive events in hockey — the winning centerman must react and drive forward in under 200ms. This drill trains the reactive start pattern: read the puck drop, explode off the back foot, and accelerate into position before the opponent. Research shows winning the faceoff in the offensive zone leads to a shot on goal 35% of the time — faceoff conditioning is directly tied to scoring.
faceoff-stance-explosive-start.transfer: Trains the explosive start from faceoff stance — centers and wingers. If you're losing draws, this is part of the answer. Strength + speed + reaction time, all in one rep.
faceoff-stance-explosive-start.cues: "Start in faceoff stance (crouched" · "Sticks on floor)" · "Explode forward on signal"
faceoff-stance-explosive-start.mistakes: Anticipating the signal instead of reacting — randomize the timing so it can't be predicted. Rising up before driving forward — stay low and drive horizontally. Weak back-foot push — the drive comes off the back foot aggressively. Only training one direction — practice winning the puck both to the forehand and backhand side.
faceoff-stance-explosive-start.progression: Progress: Add a lateral shuffle after the start to simulate taking the puck to the wall. | Regress: Non-reactive faceoff start — self-initiated explosion without the reaction component.
faceoff-stance-explosive-start.nameHint: Взрывной старт из стойки на вбрасывании
